Conceptual Questions¶

Q1. Let’s examine the differences between LDA and QDA.¶

a) If the Bayes decision boundary is linear, do we expect LDA or QDA to perform better on the training set? What about in the test set?¶

Answer:

If the Bayes Decision Boundary is Linear: Since the classes are separated by a straight line, LDA is the better choice. It is simpler, safer, and correctly models the true decision boundary.

While QDA is more flexible, it will try to introduce unnecessary curvature, leading to overfitting on the training set.

On the Test Set: If the boundary remains linear in unseen data, LDA will generalize better, while QDA may struggle due to overfitting.

LDA is the better choice in both training and test scenarios when the true decision boundary is linear.

b) If the Bayes decision boundary is non-linear, do we expect LDA or QDA to perform better on the training set? On the test set?¶

Answer:

If the Bayes Decision Boundary is Non-Linear: Since the classes are separated by a curved boundary, QDA is the better choice. It is more flexible and can adapt to the non-linear decision boundary, unlike LDA, which is restricted to straight lines.

In this case, LDA will struggle because it will try to force a linear separation when the actual boundary is curved, leading to systematic misclassification.

On the Training Set: Since QDA can model the curved boundary, it will fit the training data more accurately and is expected to perform better than LDA.

On the Test Set: If there is sufficient training data, QDA will generalize well because it correctly captures the non-linear structure. However, if the dataset is small, QDA might overfit, leading to poor generalization. In such cases, LDA may perform more reliably due to its simplicity.

QDA is generally the better choice for non-linear boundaries, but if data is limited, LDA may generalize better by avoiding overfitting.

c)In general, as the sample size n increases, do we expect the test prediction accuracy of QDA relative to LDA to improve, decline, or be unchanged? Why?¶

Answer:

As the Sample Size (n) Increases:

As the number of training samples n increases, we expect the test prediction accuracy of QDA to improve relative to LDA.

Explanation:

  • LDA is simpler model and assumes straigh line separation between classes with similar variances.
  • QDA is more flexible because it allows each class to have its own covariance matrix, making it better suited for complex, non-linear decision boundaries.
  • However, QDA estimates more parameters than LDA. With a small sample size, these estimates are unreliable because there is not enough data to compute the covariance matrices accurately, leading to overfitting and poor generalization.
  • As n increases, QDA has more data to estimate class-specific covariance matrices accurately, reducing overfitting and improving test accuracy.

Conclusion:

  • For small n: LDA performs better because it is simpler and requires fewer parameters.
  • For large n: QDA improves as it has enough data to model complex decision boundaries accurately.
  • If the true decision boundary is quadratic, QDA will eventually outperform LDA as n grows.

d)True or False:¶

Even if the Bayes decision boundary for a given problem is linear, we will probably achieve a superior test error rate using QDA rather than LDA because QDA is flexible enough to model a linear decision boundary.

Answer:

False

Explanation: QDA will introduce unnecessary complexity because it estimates separate covariance matrices for each class. If the true Bayes decision boundary is linear, then LDA is the better choice as it correctly models the decision boundary with fewer parameters.

Additionally, if the training data is small, QDA has a high risk of overfitting, making it perform worse on the test set compared to LDA, which is more stable and generalizes better.

Q2) In relation to the odds and the Default dataset¶

a) On average, what fraction of people with an odds of 0.37 of defaulting on their credit card payment will in fact default?¶

In [291]:
# BEGIN SOLUTION

def convert_odds_prob(value, to_odds = False):
    """
    Convert between odds and probability.

    Parameters:
    - value (float): The input value to convert. If converting to probability, 
                     this should be odds (O). If converting to odds, this should be probability (P).
    - to_odds (bool, optional): If True, converts probability to odds. If False (default), converts odds to probability.

    Returns:
    - float: The converted value, rounded to 4 decimal places.

    Formula:
    - To Probability:  P = O / (1 + O)  [if to_odds = False]
    - To Odds:         O = P / (1 - P)  [if to_odds = True]

    Example Usage:
    >>> convert_odds_prob(0.37)  # Convert odds to probability
    0.2701

    >>> convert_odds_prob(0.16, to_odds=True)  # Convert probability to odds
    0.1905
    """
    
    if to_odds: 
        return round(value / (1 - value), 4) # Odds = Probability / (1 - Probability)
    
    return round(value / (1 + value), 4) # Probability = Odds / (1 + Odds)

odds = 0.37
prob = convert_odds_prob(odds)
print(f"Fraction of People for {odds} Odds who will default ≈ {convert_odds_prob(odds)}", f"≈ {prob * 100:.2f}%")


# END SOLUTION

Fraction of People for 0.37 Odds who will default ≈ 0.2701 ≈ 27.01%

Answer: For 0.37 Odds the Probability of Fraud is around 27%

Q3. Suppose that we take a data set, divide it into equally sized training and test sets, and then try out two different classification procedures. First, we use logistic regression and get an error rate of 20% on the training data and 30% on the test data. Next we use 1-nearest neighbors (i.e. K=1) and get an average error rate (averaged over both test and training data sets) of 18%. Based on these results, which method should we prefer to use for classification of new observations? Why?¶

Answer:

We should prefer logistic regression over 1-nearest neighbors (K=1) for classification of new observations.

Explanation:

  1. K=1, will always get 0% training error.
    a. Since K=1 means each data point is classified based on its closest neighbor. This model is highly flexible and it will perfectly memorize the training data.
    b. Given that the average error (training + test) is 18% and the training error is 0%, the test error must be 36%, which is higher than the logistic regression test error (30%).
    c. Because it memorize the training data, even small changes in unseen observation can lead to drastically different predection.
    d. This results in overfitting, meaning the model will not generalize well to unseen data and performs poorly.

  2. Logistic Regression generalize better.
    a. Logistic regression learns a decision boundary instead of memorizing individual points, making it more robust to new data.
    b. Although the average error rate (25%) is slightly higher than the K=1 average error rate (18%), the key difference is that logistic regression has a lower test error (30%) than K=1 (36%), making it a more reliable choice.
    c. Although it has a higher training error, it avoids overfitting and provides better test accuracy than K=1.

def load_or_download_dataset(dataset_name, package, file_path):
    """
    Load a dataset from a CSV file if it exists; otherwise, download it from statsmodels and save it.

    Args:
        dataset_name (str): The name of the dataset to load from statsmodels.
        package (str): The package name where the dataset is stored.
        file_path (str): The file path to save/load the dataset.

    Returns:
        pd.DataFrame: The loaded dataset.
    """
    if not os.path.exists(file_path): 
        print(f"Downloading dataset '{dataset_name}' from statsmodels...")
        df = sm.datasets.get_rdataset(dataset_name, package).data
        df.reset_index(drop=True)
        df.to_csv(file_path, index=False)
        print(f"Dataset saved at {file_path}")
    else:
        print(f"Loading dataset from {file_path}...")
        df = pd.read_csv(file_path)

    return df

C) Compute the confusion matrix and overall fraction of correct predictions. Explain what the confusion matrix is telling you about the types of mistakes made by logistic regression.¶

In [302]:
# BEGIN SOLUTION

def evaluate_display_model(y_true, y_pred, desc, class_rpt = True):
    """
    Computes and displays classification metrics including:
    - Confusion Matrix
    - Precision
    - Recall
    - F1 Score
    - Accuracy
    - Error Rate
    - Classification Report (Conditional)
    
    Args:
    y_true (array-like): Actual class labels
    y_pred (array-like): Predicted class labels
    desc: Description to be printed as Model Stats heading
    class_rpt (bool, optional): If True (Default), displays a classification report.
    
    Returns:
    dict: A dictionary containing all computed metrics.
    """
    # Compute confusion matrix
    conf_matrix = confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred)

    # Extract True Positives (TP), False Positives (FP), False Negatives (FN), True Negatives (TN)
    TN, FP, FN, TP = conf_matrix.ravel()

    # Compute metrics
    precision = precision_score(y_true, y_pred)
    recall = recall_score(y_true, y_pred)
    f1score = f1_score(y_true, y_pred)
    accuracy = accuracy_score(y_true, y_pred)
    error_rate = 1 - accuracy
    class_report = ""
    if class_rpt:
        class_report = classification_report(y_true, y_pred, zero_division=1)

    # Print Confusion Matrix
    print(f"\n{desc} Performance:")
    print("\nConfusion Matrix:")
    print(conf_matrix)
    print(f"\nWhere:")
    print(f"TP (Actual +ve, Predicted +ve) = {TP}")
    print(f"FP (Actual -ve, Predicted +ve) = {FP}")
    print(f"FN (Actual +ve, Predicted -ve) = {FN}")
    print(f"TN (Actual -ve, Predicted -ve) = {TN}")

    # Print Other Metrics
    print(f"\nOther Metrics:")
    print(f"Precision (TP / (TP + FP)): {precision:.4f}")
    print(f"Recall (TP / (TP + FN)): {recall:.4f}")
    print(f"F1 Score (2 * (Precision * Recall) / (Precision + Recall)): {f1score:.4f}")
    print(f"Accuracy ((TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN)): {accuracy:.4f}")
    print(f"Error Rate (1 - Accuracy): {error_rate:.4f}")
    if class_rpt:
        print(f"\nClassification Report:\n{class_report}")

    # Return all metrics in a dictionary (useful for further analysis)
    return {
        "Confusion Matrix": conf_matrix,
        "Precision": precision,
        "Recall": recall,
        "F1 Score": f1score,
        "Accuracy": accuracy,
        "Error Rate": error_rate,
        "Classification Report": class_report
    }

# Call the function for evaluation

h) Which of these methods appears to provide the best results on this data?¶

Answer:

We have tested four models:

  • Logistic Regression
  • Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA)
  • Quadratic Discriminant Analysis (QDA)
  • KNN (K=1)

Below is the comparison of their performance:

Model Performance Comparison¶

Model Accuracy Precision Recall F1 Score
Logistic Regression 62.50% 62.22% 91.80% 74.17%
LDA 62.50% 62.22% 91.80% 74.17%
QDA 58.65% 58.65% 100.00% 73.94%
KNN (K=1) 50.96% 59.62% 50.82% 54.87%

Key Observations¶

  • LDA & Logistic Regression Are the Best Models on this data.
  • Both models produced identical performance metrics.
  • Both achieved 62.50% accuracy, the highest among all models.
  • Their metrics show a good balance between
    • precision ($\frac{TP}{TP + FP}$) = 62.22%
    • recall ($\frac{TP}{TP + FN}$) = 91.80%
    • F1 Score ($\frac{2 \times Precision \times Recall}{Precision + Recall}$) = 74.17%

  • Cylinders & Displacement: A clear separation is visible. Higher cylinders and displacement values correspond more often to mpg01 = 0 (lower MPG), while lower values align with mpg01 = 1 (higher MPG).
  • Horsepower & Weight: Both show strong negative associations with mpg01. Cars with high horsepower and weight are mostly in the mpg01 = 0 category.
  • Acceleration: This appears to be more evenly spread, suggesting a weaker correlation with mpg01.
  • Year: Cars from more recent years seem to have higher mpg01 values, indicating that newer cars tend to have better fuel efficiency.
  • Origin: There might be a trend, but the scatter plot isn't as clear in separating mpg01.

  • Precision is good (90%): When QDA predicts a high MPG (mpg01=1), it is correct 90% of the time.
